subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The cognitive interview was developed by Fisher and Geiselman to do what?
options: Improve the accuracy and amount of recall from eyewitnesses
questions.explain: The cognitive interview uses psychological techniques to enhance the quantity and accuracy of eyewitness recall.

questions.q: Recalling information better when in the same mood or physiological state as at learning is known as what?
questions.explain: State-dependent forgetting occurs when internal cues (mood or physical state) differ between encoding and retrieval.

questions.q: In Loftus and Palmer's second experiment, participants who heard 'smashed' were more likely to report what a week later?
options: Seeing broken glass that was not present
questions.explain: The 'smashed' group falsely recalled seeing broken glass, showing leading questions can alter the memory itself.

questions.q: A strength of the multi-store model is evidence from which type of patient?
options: Patients with internal locus of control
Amnesic patients like HM with separate STM and LTM deficits
questions.explain: Cases such as HM show STM and LTM can be damaged independently, supporting separate memory stores.

questions.q: Why might the cognitive interview be difficult to use in practice?
options: It is faster than a standard interview
It only works on procedural memory
It is time-consuming and requires special training
questions.explain: The cognitive interview takes more time and requires trained officers, making it costly to implement consistently.

questions.q: The 'weapon-focus effect' on eyewitness testimony refers to what?
options: Anxiety narrowing attention onto a weapon, reducing recall of other details
Better recall in calm conditions only
Increased recall of the perpetrator's face
questions.explain: Anxiety caused by a weapon draws attention to it, impairing recall of peripheral details like the culprit's face.

questions.q: Who proposed the multi-store model of memory?
questions.explain: The multi-store model was proposed by Atkinson and Shiffrin in 1968.

questions.q: Which type of long-term memory stores personal events and experiences with a time-stamp?
questions.explain: Episodic memory holds time-stamped autobiographical events such as a recent birthday.

questions.q: The Yerkes-Dodson law suggests the relationship between anxiety and eyewitness accuracy is what?
options: An inverted-U, with moderate arousal optimal
questions.explain: The Yerkes-Dodson inverted-U suggests memory accuracy peaks at moderate arousal and declines at very low or very high anxiety.

questions.q: Tulving distinguished three types of long-term memory. Which is correct?
questions.explain: Tulving proposed episodic, semantic and procedural long-term memories.

questions.q: The phonological loop is subdivided into which two parts?
questions.explain: The phonological loop comprises the phonological store (inner ear) and the articulatory process (inner voice).

questions.q: Retroactive interference occurs when what happens?
options: A cue triggers an unwanted memory
New information disrupts recall of previously stored information
questions.explain: In retroactive interference, newly learned information disrupts the recall of older memories.

questions.q: Which best describes 'chunking' in relation to short-term memory?
options: Grouping items into meaningful units to increase effective capacity
questions.explain: Chunking combines individual items into larger meaningful units, increasing the amount STM can hold.

questions.q: Knowledge of facts, concepts and the meaning of words is stored in which memory type?
questions.explain: Semantic memory holds shared general knowledge of facts, concepts and meanings.

questions.q: Memory for how to perform skills such as riding a bike is which type of LTM?
questions.explain: Procedural memory stores motor skills and actions performed largely without conscious effort.

questions.q: Which factor reduces the accuracy of eyewitness testimony through post-event discussion?
questions.explain: Discussing an event with co-witnesses can contaminate memory, causing witnesses to conform to each other's accounts.

questions.q: Which type of long-term memory is described as the most explicit and requires conscious recall of details?
questions.explain: Episodic memory is explicit and requires conscious effort to recall specific events.

questions.q: Recalling information best when in the same physical environment as when it was learned is an example of what?
questions.explain: Context-dependent retrieval shows recall improves when external cues at retrieval match those at encoding (e.g. Godden and Baddeley's divers).

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the four techniques of the cognitive interview?
questions.explain: 'Report everything' encourages witnesses to recall all details, even seemingly trivial ones, which may trigger other memories.

questions.q: Coding in short-term memory is primarily which form, according to Baddeley?
questions.explain: Baddeley found STM is mainly coded acoustically, as acoustically similar words were harder to recall in order.

questions.q: Logie subdivided the visuo-spatial sketchpad into which two parts?
questions.explain: Logie split the sketchpad into the visual cache (stores visual data) and the inner scribe (records arrangement).

questions.q: The case of patient KF, who had poor verbal STM but intact visual STM, challenged the MSM by suggesting what?
options: Coding in STM is always semantic
STM has multiple components, as in the working memory model
STM is a single unitary store
questions.explain: KF's selective deficit suggests STM is not unitary, supporting the multiple components of the working memory model.

questions.q: Proactive interference occurs when what happens?
options: Older information disrupts recall of newer information
New information disrupts recall of older information
Information decays in the sensory register
questions.explain: In proactive interference, previously learned information disrupts the recall of more recently learned information.

questions.q: In the working memory model, the phonological loop deals with which type of information?
questions.explain: The phonological loop processes auditory and speech-based (verbal) information.

questions.q: The cognitive interview technique of 'reinstate the context' is based on which memory principle?
questions.explain: Mentally recreating the scene provides contextual cues, drawing on context-dependent retrieval to aid recall.

questions.q: The cognitive interview technique of recalling events in a different order helps because it does what?
options: Reduces the influence of prior expectations or schema on recall
questions.explain: Changing the recall order disrupts schema-driven expectations, reducing reconstructed or dishonest reporting.

questions.q: Interference is most likely to cause forgetting when the two sets of information are what?
questions.explain: Interference effects are strongest when the competing memories are similar, as McGeoch and McDonald showed.

questions.q: According to research, what is the duration of the short-term memory store?
questions.explain: STM has a limited duration of roughly 18-30 seconds without rehearsal, as shown by Peterson and Peterson.

questions.q: What is the widely accepted capacity of short-term memory according to Miller?
questions.explain: Miller's 'magic number' suggests STM holds about 7 plus or minus 2 items or chunks.

questions.q: Retrieval failure as an explanation for forgetting is based on which principle?
questions.explain: Tulving's encoding specificity principle states recall is best when cues present at encoding are also present at retrieval.
